utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning. We shall go into closed session while the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Tanic. I have a number of matters to deal with before your evidence recommences, and I'll deal with these now. Mr. Visnjic, the United Kingdom have applied again for an extension of time to respond to your 54 bis motion. Are you content that they have more time to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are content, Your Honour. We were going through the documentation received, and it may be that our request has been met in full. But at this moment, I cannot say that for certain, since we are still studying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be then that we will extend the time indefinitely and leave it to you to draw it to our attention if the motion is to proceed. But there will be a written order to a that if that's what we decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The second matter is that an application has been made for protective measures in relation to K56. In view of the date proposed for the witness to give evidence, the Defence should respond to that by Friday of this week, that's the 17th. And the final matter relates to the evidence we were considering at the close of business on Friday; the question of the admissibility of the hearsay evidence relating to what was said by others about the accused Mr. Sainovic. The Trial Chamber has found this an extremely difficult matter to resolve, and we'll ultimately decided that this evidence is admissible. But the weight to be given to evidence of this nature, touching as it does on an important element, which could contribute to the evidence of individual criminal responsibility of this accused, is quite another matter. And it will give us further considerable food for thought in due course, but for the moment the decision is to hear this evidence. Now, Mr. Tanic, your evidence will continue. Mr. Hannis will continue with his examination. The solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today and throughout if you should return tomorrow to continue, then the solemn declaration will also continue to apply. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 2 Q. Good morning, Mr. Tanic. When we finished on Friday, I think we had just talked about a fact-finding mission to Kosova that was undertaken by General Perisic and Jovica Stanisic. Do you recall approximately when that mission occurred?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in early 1998, but I believe you can find the exact period in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if it occurred before the attack on the Adem Jashari family compound?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes. But you should check that against my statement; I don't have any dates which I could consult here before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you indicated that Mr. Sainovic went on that trip. Before he joined them, do you know from General Perisic or Mr. Stanisic if they had previously planned to ask some other representative of the government to accompany them on that trip?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, having heard that from General Perisic, they planned to bring along Mr. Zoran Lilic. They wanted his participation in the effort so as to strengthen it, to strengthen the efforts to try and avoid the war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why they had a preference for Mr. Lilic over Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic is an honest person who enjoy the reputation of one of the top political officials who was advocating for a political solution which would avoid the war, which couldn't be said for Mr. Sainovic. This is what I was told by Mr. Perisic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After that fact-finding mission, did you know if Perisic and/or Stanisic made any recommendations to Slobodan Milosevic about Kosovo? First of all, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how do you know that? What was your source?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that only from Perisic, but I knew that at the time through various channels, through my party's leadership, and other sources. I had known about their recommendations before I spoke about the mission with Perisic. The recommendations were public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall for the Court now what some of those recommendations were?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and basic one was for the KLA to be declared officially a terrorist organisation, because up until then the KLA was referred to as a terrorist organisation only per se or colloquially; so it differs, the unofficial and the official qualification. Another recommendation, including the entire territory of Kosovo, was to introduce the state of emergency, which would enable legitimate use of the army and of the special police units which were capable to separate the terrorists from the civilian population. The third recommendation was to implement, as quickly as possible, the already existing political situation resolution for Kosovo. That was for Milosevic to sign and everyone knew in Belgrade that in existence, which included the basic autonomy for Kosovo, and holding of elections, and building up of confidence. Those measures were supposed to be put in a package and it was believed that that would have sufficed to deal with the problem of terrorism; that is to separate it from the political issues situation in Kosovo and to try and deal with these two situations in parallel; to try at the same time to avoid the war with Kosovo Albanians and with the international community, and to minimise casualties on both sides. This was in keeping with some recommendations made previously by the leadership of my party and Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if any of those recommendations were followed by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Neither he nor his associates. The KLA was never officially declared a terrorist organisation at that time. The state of emergency was never introduced, which would have enabled the legitimate use of the army and the police. And some decisions were made subsequently within the commission for Kosovo as regards the use of the special police forces, but this went through a -- sort of a private chain of command so to say. As far as the political solution of the problem, well, neither Milosevic nor the people around him wanted to hear anything about the agreement, and in this way they simply provided for a radicalisation of the Albanian popular opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the answer you just gave you said that one of the goals of those recommendations was to minimise casualties on both sides in Kosovo. What was happening in Kosovo that was resulting in casualties in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, first and foremost, there was an unprofessional use of police units in place, which were used to combat terrorism. Albanian terrorists had this habit of mingling with civilians, which is the strategy used by terrorists all over the world. But that is why you have special police measures in place, which enable for the distinction between the civilians and the terrorists. Instead of that, unfortunately, our units often undertook measures and carried out actions, trying to eliminate or remove terrorists. But they would do that en masse with many civilian casualties, although the police had known that there would be civilian casualties. Of course there were casualties on our side as well, within our police, but there was a private chain of command going from Milosevic through his channels, which resulted in an informational chaos and, of course, the increasing number of casualties on both side. It wasn't known exactly how the army could have been used since there was no state of emergency. And they were used here and there, and that was contrary to the constitution. This led the country to an even a graver situation and at the same time feeding the Albanian extremism. I didn't participate in any combat down there; therefore, I cannot speak of any specific crimes. But this impression was not shared by me but by some other people as well. And I'm pretty sure that the chiefs of the armed forces and the security forces shared that view. The greatest problem was that parallel chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect for the Chamber, I don't know where this line of questioning is taking us. Again, we have impressions, opinions; we are not given a source. I've never seen such a testimony up until now, and I don't know where this will take us. Just to remind you, Judge May shared my views during the last testimony of this witness. Please take a look at the words he uses. I really don't know where this is taking us, and this is what I object to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I had sources of information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please be quiet while we deal with this matter. You'll get your opportunity to speak further when questioned further. Anything else, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you. I just wanted to point out what bothered me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask a couple of questions to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with the objection that suggests that this is rambling recollections of the witness that aren't really focused on the issues that we're dealing with in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this particular question had to deal with the issue of civilian casualties in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it didn't give us very much information about it, did it? The other thing it's raised is what's described as a parallel command structure, which has just appeared out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's non-responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's of -- and it's gone forever, the answer, without really taking -- advancing the case. So we need a much more focussed examination, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll make my best efforts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, with regard to the question of civilian casualties among the Kosovo Albanians in 1998, was that a state secret?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the better part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wasn't it also well publicised in the media?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some cases were published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was the issue of the casualties to Kosovo Albanian civilians brought to Mr. Milosevic's attention? First of all, just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was that done? If you could tell us by whom, and how did they bring it to his attention.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was first done by us, the leadership of our party, but as far as I know General Perisic and Mr. Stanisic pointed it out on behalf of their official services within their capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you, in New Democracy, bring it to his attention?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In written form, but there must have been conversations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally ever have a conversation with Mr. Milosevic about this matter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must join with Mr. Fila about these answers. The answer 8, line 14 "There must have been conversations as well." That's not at all helpful, and is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's obviously the case, Mr. Ackerman, but Mr. Hannis appreciates that, too. And it's plain from his next question that he's dealing with the issue. It may not advance any further, but he has chosen to spend his Prosecution time on endeavouring to get evidence from this witness. And he now realises he has to focus on particular points, and I think he's trying to do that at the moment. How we assess evidence later is another a matter. And if he fails and tries to remain satisfied with the vague answer you've referred to, of course we'll address the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just think his impressions and must haves and must have beens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, I think Mr. Hannis realises that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- are just useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you said you did have a conversation with Mr. Milosevic about that. Can you tell us approximately when that occurred and where it occurred.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, don't go any further than that answer because Mr. Hannis is asking you about 1998. So he'll want to address a different question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say you had a conversation before 1998. Was that conversation about the issue of Kosovo Albanian civilians in police operations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It concerned the way for resolving the problem. Since terrorism in the second half of 1997 began its growth, it became stronger. And already there was discussion in place how to distinguish or to separate civilians from the rest. It is very difficult for me to speak without my notes. I would like to check some dates, and I don't even have my statement in front of me; therefore, I'm asked to recall things that took place a decade ago and then the Defence can abuse that. Therefore, without my own statement, it's difficult for me to recall the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Set aside the date for a moment. Would you tell us what the substance of that conversation was regarding separating terrorists from civilians and how to distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said, the whole story has been repeating -- had been repeating itself for months and years, the political solution, the declaring of the KLA a terrorist organisation, the dispatch of special forces, the proclamation of the state of emergency. These things in Serbian political life --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please listen to the question you're being asked and answer the question you are being asked. Do not go over matters you've already told us about in very general terms, because Mr. Hannis is trying to pin down specific facts for our consideration. So please assist him. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you answered earlier that -- I think it was in the second half of 1997, that there was already discussion in place how to distinguish or separate civilians from the rest. Did you have a conversation with Mr. Milosevic about that problem?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a brief one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he said about that.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He simply said that the Albanian population supports the terrorists and that the problem is in the numbers of Albanians; and that that should be brought down to a reasonable figure, but we are not discussing Milosevic here I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, we've reached a stage where I think I have to talk to you more seriously about the purpose of bringing you here. It's to hear your evidence in answer to questions that counsel choose to ask you. It's not to hear what you wish to tell us. And it's not for you to decide whether questions relating to Milosevic are relevant to this trial or not. Please confine yourself to answering the questions that are asked of you, then we'll make some progress. Because you ought to also bear in mind that the Prosecution have a limited amount of time available to them in the big wide world to present this case, and there's great international concern about how long these trials take. So we are endeavouring to make progress, focusing on the facts that will assist us to resolve the issues presented by the indictment. Please assist the Trial Chamber in doing that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, did you have any conversations with General Perisic about the recommendations he had made, Slobodan Milosevic, about the problem in Kosovo province?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when and where you had those conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that conversation, did he show you a letter he had written to Mr. Milosevic setting forth his complaints and suggested recommendations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we bring up Exhibit P17, please -- I'm sorry, it should be 717. I think I misspoke, 717.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in discussing that letter with him, did he tell you whether or not Mr. Milosevic had acted favourably on any of his recommendations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He conveyed to me Milosevic's comment, which however was not a positive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have the English on the screen for us, and the B/C/S for the witness. And if we can go to page 2 of the B/C/S for the witness -- I'm sorry, page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that on the screen, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's General Perisic's warning letter at the time he was the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslav. It is addressed to Milosevic, informing him on what is really happening and what problems there are in connection with the Kosovo conflict. It's identical to other letters sent by us and the security services, which I have already referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could look at the first -- on the first page, items listed 1 through 6 which were described by Mr. Perisic's certain negative facts, including the tendency to use the VJ outside institutions of the system, separating VJ units from the army, attempt to command VJ units by unauthorised persons. Did you discuss each of these with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's very exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page of the B/C/S and keep that same English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, perhaps you can help us with what I think is an error in translation on the English version or a missing word. On the B/C/S version at the top under number 1(A), can you read us that first line.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been resolved." First it says: "1, tendency of the use of the army outside the institutions of the system" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The situation in Kosovo and Metohija" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please read more slowly because with something in front of you the tendency is to speed up your speech. Read from A again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The situation in Kosovo and Metohija could have been resolved by introducing a state of emergency on time on the 20th of April, 1998, when I sent you a written proposal attachment number 1. As you did not take this into account" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the word "emergency" is missing from the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, in item (b) there is a reference that's translated in the English as a session of the "BSO," can you tell us what the BSO is. There is an explanation in the English translation, but I want to be sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see on the transcript, it appears I spoke B-, as in boy, S-O, but it's V-, as in Victor, S-O. And at the bottom of that paragraph (b) General Perisic explains three reasons why the use of the VJ in this way is untenable. His proposed resolution, can you read that for us?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Such further use of the Army of Yugoslavia - VJ is Army of Yugoslavia - is untenable for at least three reasons. First" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll stop you there. Can you go below that and read what the proposed resolution General Perisic made was.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see it, so I can't. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We have to scroll down on the B/C/S for you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Proposal of solution: Use the Army of Yugoslavia legally to defend the border belt, military facilities, and units; do not use it for other tasks or declare one of the situations provided for by the constitution and use it in its full force. The position is clear to us, but we have to have a legal political decision. Because if the Federal Assembly or the cabinet of the Republic of Yugoslavia does not want to or is not capable of reaching it, who has the right to take on such responsibility. "2, separating units from the VJ" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to point 2, he does complain about the Guards Brigade having been separated by Mr. Milosevic's decision. Do you know anything about that? What was the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'm not competent to respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page then of the B/C/S and stay on the current page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 3 is a complaint about the attempt to command the VJ by unauthorised persons. And in paragraph 3(a), he gives an example or refers to the example of Decani and Orahovac. Do you have any information or knowledge about what happened in Decani or Orahovac related to this attempt to command by unauthorised persons? He's describing the desire by members of the MUP to subordinate a VJ unit.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through this private chain of command, through this Commission For Kosovo, which later renamed its into the Commission for the Fight Against Terrorism; so through this parallel chain of command, instructions arrived from Belgrade saying that the army should give the police mortars, 120-millimetres, rocket-launchers, and other equipment which under our laws, let alone the Geneva Convention, are banned. They're prohibited for use against civilians unless there is a state of emergency. General Perisic, as he told me, as he was facing problems of this kind, more than once he prohibited this. And also an operative of the security service told me that the MUP had asked for the army to intervene, and the army had done so in a manner that was of no use in the struggle against terrorism but produced civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go to the next paragraph, 3(b) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, are we to hear more about the Commission for Kosovo and the Commission for the Fight Against Terrorism?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3(b) speaks about the attempt by the civilian part of staff to command the corps, and he states that the responsibility of the corps commander is to evaluate the situation, plan operations for the VJ and the MUP in cooperation with civilian members of the staff and the MUP, and report to Sainovic and Minic. First of all, can you tell us who Minic was. Milomir Minic was also one of Milosevic's closest collaborators, just like Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did Mr. Minic have a position in the government?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to recall now. I'm sure he did, but it's hard to recall precisely what it was. Mr. Perisic was referring to the two of them as members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you know about this commission? Was your source of information about the commission from General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I knew about the commission previously when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall now approximately when it was established, and how you first learned about it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about its existence at the time it was established, as far as I can recall. I don't have my notes before me so it's difficult to recall the time. I think it was in late 1997 or early 1998. In any case, it was at the time when Milosevic with his collaborators rejected a political solution for Kosovo, as he was unable to ensure implementation of his policy through legal channels because there was resistance to that, as people knew that a political solution existed. So as he could not gain through the legal political institutions, he established this parallel institution, the Commission for Kosovo, the members of which were Sainovic, Minic, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where in the statement is this referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The commission, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is -- let me check my note. Just a minute. In paragraphs, I think, somewhere between 81 and 85. I think beginning at 82 describes the creation of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So this is under a different name, but nevertheless it's a commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you recall in our opening statement, we mention there was a body referred to by two or three names, which we believe the evidence will show is the same body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give the Trial Chamber a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, on a number of occasions you've referred to not having access here to your notes. Did you actually have handwritten notes you made at the time of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm referring to my statement of 1999 and early 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, the Chamber is tentatively of the view that dealing -- where we're dealing with so many issues over a long period of time so long after the events, that it may be appropriate for the witness to have the statement there, so that we can be fully informed of these events; bearing in mind, of course, that he would be assisted to some extent by a statement made on an earlier occasion. But it may be contrary to the interests of justice to prevent that clarification that could be obtained from reference to the statement. Would you wish to comment on that before we make a final decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness was originally scheduled to be a live witness, in which case there would have been no statement before him. He was then made a 92 ter/live, and your ruling was he could have the statement for the first 45 paragraphs. We say that, in the interests of justice, one of the things you must be able to evaluate is this man's credibility, honesty, and trustworthiness. And he was scheduled to be a live witness; you've ruled he is to be a live witness for this portion of his testimony. And we say a fundamental part of the evaluation of the evidence will go to the weight you will give it, based on his credibility, ability to recollect, and be truthful. So we say his statement should not be put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the other hand, we are requiring of people recollection of events, which in the case of the evidence we are at the moment are over eight years ago. And recollection, as know, does fade with the passage of time. And there is an intervening period at which he has required to concentrate on his recollection of events and record matters, which might assist him to give us a more accurate, full account at this stage. Now, this is different -- this is quite different from the decision we made earlier, which was that as a substitute for his evidence we would not be -- his oral evidence, we would not be prepared to consider the bulk of the statement. So there is an issue here over whether, in fact, preventing reference to something that is his own document would act contrary to the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I won't repeat the point I made. But of course he was proofed by the Prosecutor on the 4th and 5th of November with that document. He came to court on Friday with that document. He may in fact have re-read his full statement over the weekend; you can ask him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I'm being invited by counsel to ask you whether in fact you read your statement again over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I made no effort to memorise the dates. I was looking at the processes and events. I do not want the Defence to challenge me because I may mistake a date. I am talking about political events, but I cannot commit to memory all those dates and times. They will then stand up and say, no, the commission was not established in late 1997 but in early 1998; so you, Tanic, know nothing about this. However, I did not try to memorise the dates because I did not think I would be able to consult my own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours, I have two grounds. First, in paragraph 53, the state commission is mentioned for the first time. But it seems that Mr. Hannis doesn't like this because it is linked to certain events. So let's take a good look at paragraph 53, and what he says there about when it was established. Secondly, the witness was able to see his statement over the weekend. And as Mr. Hannis kept adding on to what the witness was to testify to, we have two additional requests or motions for alterations even to 65 ter. And let's be thorough. And if the witness makes a mistake of a few months, we will accept that, and nobody is expecting him to give the precise date. Of course, such small discrepancies can be tolerated. But he keeps putting forward new information, and we want to check his credibility. Inter alia, look at paragraph 53 and you will see when the commission was established. And Mr. Hannis is reading another paragraph which fits in with what the witness is saying. I am opposed to the witness having the statement before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just add what we are trying to assess here is the witness's ability to transmit faithfully what he heard from others. I think we have the problem right now that he cannot even faithfully convey what he himself produced. Just to add to what Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Fila has said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, this is an insult. I know that as a witness I don't have the right to speak out, but this is an insult that I'm unable to convey what I did myself. It's a serious insult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, just please bear with us while we consider these issues. Counsel have duties to explain to me fully the basis on which they wish to oppose the matter that we are considering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, if I may. This general issue is one that's very near to my head and heart. I used to have an excellent memory, I'm told. I don't have a personal recollection of that anymore. Sometimes I don't remember what I had for supper last night or whether I showered under my arms, but this is a problem for all Courts and all Tribunals dealing with witnesses, particularly witnesses talking about events that happened long ago. In my jurisdiction there are a couple of ways of dealing with that. One talks about remembrance refreshed, in which case if a witness has made. A statement on a prior occasion closer in time to the events, he's given the opportunity to look at it. He's asked if having looked at it refreshes his memory. If it does, he sets it aside and he describes what he remembers now having been refreshed. On the other hand, he may look at it and say: "Well, I know I gave a statement five, six, eight years ago, and at the time the events were fresh in my memory. But reading it now, it doesn't refresh my memory. But I know at the time, it was fresh in my mind, and I gave a true account at that time." In that event, the actual statement itself is permitted as his evidence, as opposed to his testimony. But in either situation, Your Honour, I think in the interests of justice in this Tribunal's effort to search for the truth, it would not be unfair to the Defence or to the of this Tribunal to allow the witness to refer to his statement and see if it does refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We propose to give a ruling on this in the absence of the witness. So we'll need to go into closed session while he leaves the court until we make our ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we consider that giving the witness the statement for the purpose of referring generally to its contents to refresh his memory would not advance the interests of justice here and essentially would be contrary to the decision we made earlier in relation to the statement. However, it's plain that there will be occasions - and there may already have been occasions - where for the sake of accuracy in the sequence of events and the exact content of discussions, it would be helpful for the statement to be available to refresh his recollection. So we will be sympathetic to the suggestion that he should be directed to particular passages in the sort of situation you've identified, but we're not satisfied that he could -- simply where he claimed a general lack of recollection of an event or a -- or a sequence of events under a topic be allowed to do so. It would be allowed for specific purposes as we go along. Therefore, we feel that his evidence will be enhanced by hearing it live without that assistance so far as possible. So please bear these thoughts in mind. Direct our attention to occasions where you feel it would assist. We may even identify them ourselves, but we do not think the witness should at any stage be given the impression that general reference to the statement will be permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go back into closed session now while the witness is brought back into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, we've made a ruling and we'll proceed on the basis of that ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On the exhibit presently now on the screen, if we could go to the next page of the English and scroll up a bit on the current page of B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, before we digress for a bit, we were talking about General Perisic's letter and paragraph 3, where he was complaining about the attempts by some civilian parties to command the VJ. And in paragraph 3, he had talked about -- that in practice, the commander of the Pristina Corps plans what he's ordered to do, which is at the request of Sainovic, Minic, and the MUP, and it is then turned into the service for planning and realisation. Did General Perisic tell you anything about problems resulting from that practice?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me what he had written down. He said the result is that the Army of Yugoslavia is used inefficiently and that there are many casualties and that there were poor results. As for Sainovic and Minic, they conveyed orders to the MUP as well, and I knew that before Perisic told me. Those two men truly transmitted Milosevic's messages so as to be able to make decisions within the army and the police. I had known that previously, whereas Mr. Perisic has confirmed this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what was the source of your information about this before you heard it from General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Security Service and some well-meaning Milosevic's collaborators, the head of my party as well. There were three or four different sources of different levels, but they all confirmed the same thing, including the international participation factor, but I guess this is not the time to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me then go to paragraph 4, which regarded bypassing levels of command in conducting official talks and distributing assignments. General Perisic complained that Mr. Milosevic sometimes had -- even though as commander in certain states, he had the right to speak to anybody in the VJ. General Perisic complained that this was done without the knowledge of the Chief of Staff of the army. And who was the Chief of Staff of the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, related to this problem, did General Perisic tell you anything about steps that he personally had taken in 1998 to keep control and know what the VJ units in Kosovo were doing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He ordered a written order, stating that not a single piece of equipment by the army, especially heavy artillery and heavy equipment, cannot be moved an inch on anyone's request, be it Sainovic, Minic, or the MUP, without his consent. Since many tricks were used. People would say, Move your tank by one metre. And by having done that the tank could target a civilian house, whereas the army personnel would be ignorant to that. Therefore, he prohibited this in writing such use of army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did General Perisic tell you whether or not that step had been effective in eliminating the problem?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that it was efficient for a short while, but then General Perisic was replaced; and at that same time Mr. Stanisic left his position, as well as his deputy Mijatovic. This is all to do with similar problems, and this all tallies with what I discussed with Mijatovic as regards the State Security Service. Their view was identical to the view of the Army of Yugoslavia, the opinion of how Milosevic was trying to provoke a war down there. And in their views, Sainovic and Minic figured as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You spoke in one of your earlier answers about the -- I forget the term you used, but it had to do with going outside the chain of command or an illegal chain of command. Do you recall -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, colloquially, we call it the private chain of command. Of course, it is illegal. We just refer to it as private. All of us who knew about its existence, we called it the private Sloba's chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What can you tell the Court about the private chain of command. Can you give us an example of how that worked and who was involved?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards civilian figures, there was Sainovic and Minic for internal affairs; Milutinovic in his relation with the community, with the international community, but this is another side of the matter. Since Milosevic could not procure institutional support for the war in Kosovo, since there was political solution in existence, he assembled a group of his friends. And then they issued directives to the police; they would provide false information. They would say there are few terrorists there, go intervene and arrest them. And as it turns out, there were far more terrorists and our policemen would get killed. This is the traitor policy mentioned by Perisic. And then some casualties were used by Milosevic so as to create the spiral of violence. This was initiated by the Jashari incident in Prekaz, and then it continued in several other instances. I didn't participate in any of these cases, but the information I have is credible. This was done in that way. First, there would be Serbian casualties which were planned, so as to provoke a mass response, and then we would have a slaughterhouse. The spiral of violence evolved and the Albanian terrorists could hardly wait for it. They would say, "Yes. You see, we have to fight for freedom." That's how Milosevic turned Albanian terrorists into freedom fighters together with his friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, a journalist could have been written that, and it would have got the same value from us as any piece of journalistic nature. If that's to come of any value, there's going to need to be meat put on the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, did Mr. Perisic give you any examples of how this private chain of command had worked with regard to the VJ, if indeed there had had been any instances of that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I described. Sainovic would pick up a phone. He would say, "Move your tank by two metres." This was exactly as I described. As His Honour said, a journalist could write that, but my information was far more credible. And an operative from the security service specified the very similar example in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Did General Perisic become aware of anyone under his command who was operating in response to that private chain of command without his knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it was Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he tell you -- did General Perisic tell you whether he had taken any steps to try and discipline Pavkovic for that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't specify the steps; and shortly afterwards, he was from his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was removed? Pavkovic or Perisic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, were there any specific examples given to you of General Pavkovic responding to this informal chain of command or unofficial chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he told me that he reacted by way of several oral warnings to Milosevic; and when that heeded no result he put it in writing, which at that time was proclaimed a state secret, and it was never published anywhere as far as I know. And then we know what followed, he lost his job. For a while, his written orders were in place prohibiting the use of army pieces; but after he was removed, it all crumbled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless you've misunderstood me, it must be that you don't have any such information. I was anxious to know if you could give examples of conduct of General Pavkovic that was in response to something ordered by the unofficial chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The fault is mine. I misunderstood. You were referring to Pavkovic rather than Perisic. I apologise to the Bench. As far as General Perisic told me, Pavkovic had an inclination to take Sainovic's orders and to engage military units to assist the MUP and to give them to use mortars and tanks within a limited scope, but nevertheless contrary to constitutional provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't have any specific examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He wasn't specific. Our conversation was just to exchange information, and I knew about that from other sources. I know of an example in Decani, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- during 1998 or 1999, did you, in your dealings with the SDB, come across information about something called Operation Horseshoe; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the SDB, but from Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the same time you were having this discussion with him, when he showed you the letter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were three long conversations, five to six hours each.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, what did he tell you about Operation Horseshoe? What was it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said what I knew, that our military had plans for exercises simulating various situations. And it was a nickname for the plan, the horseshoe. It wasn't its official name; it was a contingency plan of the former JNA from the times of Tito. And it's possible for such contingencies as an attack from the south-east. And provided the Albanian population sided with the aggressor, there were six or seven axes to be used to eliminate potential Albanian strongholds, which were used by an outside enemy. This is a regular contingency plan that any army has, and it foresaw seven directions which would form a horseshoe; hence the nickname of the plan, although, I repeat, it wasn't its official title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know its official title?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't go into such detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about in, approximately, October of 1998, do you recall attending a reception at the German embassy?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is in my statement, then I did attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Do you know a Vladimir Stambuk?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You refreshed my recollection now. I know the gentleman and I know what you're referring to. It was a reception --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you tell us about that. Tell the Judges who he was and what his position was.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir Stambuk holds a Ph.D. He was the main ideologist of the United Yugoslav Left, the so-called JUL, led by Milosevic's spouse, Mira Markovic. He was one of her closest collaborators, and he was part of his inner circle. When I say his "inner circle," I mean his immediate circle of contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what position he held in the government, if any?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to recall. I used to know several hundred people. I think he had a position. I believe he was one of the deputies of the government. But if I am mistaken, I'm asking not to be abused on this piece of information by the Defence, so that this information is not abused. In any case, he was a influential person among the so-called Hawks in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any unusual comment or remark he made at that reception in your presence?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was very unusual; therefore, I had to try and intervene, to try and stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us who else was present when he made this remark.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British ambassador, Donnelly, and the German ambassador, Gruber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four of us; Stambuk, the two aforementioned ambassadors, and I. And I did my best to carry a conversation with the ambassadors to try and convince them not to bomb Yugoslavia. And Stambuk appeared and said literally, "Well, we wouldn't mind a few bombs by NATO." And the two ambassadors were astounded, jaws aslaver. They were surprised to hear a leader of a political elite saying he had nothing against that. He said that our authorities wouldn't object against some bombing, a little bit of it. It was almost unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you subsequently have a one-on-one conversation that same evening with Mr. Stambuk about that remark?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took him to the side as far as I could. I asked Gruber and Donnelly to dismiss that remark. They looked at me in surprise, because this was something punishable by jail sentence according to our law. I asked Stambuk what came to him, what he meant by saying that we wouldn't mind having a bit of war. Since we were on good terms, he explained to me the doctrine. He said that I was stupid, together with the president of my party, Mihajlovic, for having left the government. He said that a few bombs by the NATO pact could be a very good excuse to eliminate our position, to cleanse the Albanians. And since our factories were not operational, we could use that as the excuse as well. It was a doctrine. He tried to put forth the advantages we could gain by some bombing our country. I was amazed, since I never heard any such thing in my career, not in such clear terms and so specifically. Therefore, I asked him, "Did you ever discuss this with anyone or is this your private position?" And he said it was the family position. And he mention Milosevic and Mira and a few friends of theirs, and he said again that Dusan and I shouldn't be dumb, that we should return to the government, and that there will be some war, and that we can use it to our advantage. It was an unbelievable conversation. I put together a document on the conversation and sent it to the state security, since this was treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anything happen as a result of that report you sent to the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. The operative told me they have knowledge of certain statements of that nature from Milosevic's collaborators, that there were people going around saying, "Well, a bit of war couldn't do any harm." They were quite astounded, too. But I believe at that time Stanisic was no longer the head of the service; I believe it was Markovic. And their hands were tied. Many people were afraid for their positions. Nothing came of it. But they did confirm that they received such information from various sources; therefore, this was no news to them. We were sort of completely taken aback.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the end of October 1998, there was an agreement reached between Mr. Milosevic and Holbrooke and some related agreements that established the Kosovo Verification Mission. Around that time, do you recall any changes in the top personnel in Mr. Milosevic's regime?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, and I don't have my notes. Can you rephrase, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've already mentioned a couple of people being replaced. And I guess my question is: Did this happen at that time? You mentioned General Perisic being replaced and Mr. Stanisic. Do you recall approximately when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. It was shortly after the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was selected to replace General Perisic as the Chief of Staff for the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavkovic, General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you certain about that, Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise. You're right. Pavkovic was commander of the Pristina Corps. It is Dragoljub Ojdanic; he was to replace Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before going any further on that, can I have a date roughly for the reception where this conversation took place, Mr. Tanic, that's the conversation with Stambuk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in my statement, I believe. It can be checked. Would you be so kind as to remind me again, refresh my memory. I remember processes, sequences of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You -- the conversation included reference to some bombing would not be unwelcome. When was it in relation to the start of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know now. Thank you, Your Honour. It was at the time when desperate attempts were made so as to avoid the bombing; therefore, it was one to two months before the conflict with NATO; at the most, one or two months prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it's time for our first break. So you -- well, first of all we'll go into closed session before you leave the courtroom, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in light of the last question that you put to the witness concerning the timing of that event at the German embassy reception, I would, with your permission, like to be able to show the witness his statement and refer him to paragraph 94 and ask him if that refreshes his memory about the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the thing to do is to put the specific point to the witness from the statement, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, at the time you made your statement, I would indicate to you that in paragraph 94 you date the embassy event as October of 1998. You answered Judge Bonomy earlier that you thought it was maybe no more than one or two months before the bombing which started in March. Now, after having heard what you reported in your statement, how do you resolve that difference? Which one do you think is more correct, and why?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought about it during the break, and I'm sure that the one from October 1998 is more correct. I placed this within the time-frame of two months before the bombing; whereas, in fact it was three or four months before the bombing. I do apologise, but there were hundreds and hundreds of meetings and conversations. October 1998 is correct to the best of my recollection, but it can be checked, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As early as October 1998, were people in Serbia talking about the possibility of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got this information from the most credible western sources seven months before the bombing, and I conveyed it to the security service. They took it seriously; and later on, it transpired that there was more such information. So that the inner circle, the political elite, in Serbia, to which I belonged, knew that if no political solution was found for Kosovo, most likely there would be an intervention by NATO. It wasn't the general public in Serbia who discussed this, but only a certain inner circle of politicians, intelligence agents, and so on. The general public were afraid that the conflict might break out, but they didn't have this information. I apologise for mistaking the time, but that's due to the large number of events taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For Defence counsel and the Court, I'm going to paragraph 86 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you have any personal knowledge about the involvement of any of the accused in events related to an incident that occurred in mid-January 1999 in Racak?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This matter is no longer part of our indictment, and evidence should not be led in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not offering this for the purposes of showing the killing incident, but rather we argue it goes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need go no further. I mean, I've read this before, considered the point already. I hear what Mr. O'Sullivan has to say, but this evidence is relevant to the issue of individual criminal responsibility. And I note your assurance that you're not going into the episode itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to this unfortunate incident, I discussed it with the State Security Service and also with the president of my party, Mihajlovic, as we knew that this was a direct escalation of the conflict. I was informed by the service that, according to the scenario I have already described, there was simply confusing information reaching the ground for Mr. Sainovic; that the Jashari brothers, who were criminals and smugglers, could have been arrested by our units previously, but they were not allowed to do so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think from -- I think if you just stop there you may be talking about -- you may be talking at cross-purposes with Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's intervention. Maybe I need to ask another question here. I think I also understand what the answer was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, the event regarding the Jashari brothers occurred much earlier than this Racak event; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My mistake because of the large number of events. Racak, yes, there is a tape originating from Serb sources, the State Security Service sources. It was acquired through operations of interception of communications. And one can hear on that tape that Mr. Sainovic is exchanging opinions and giving certain instructions to Mr. Lukic in connection with combat operations in this village, and later on the removal of traces. I was able to listen to this tape; and later on through Serb sources, it was partly made public, to point out what problems were arising from the parallel chain of command. Later on I received confirmation from western sources that they also had tapes showing that Mr. Sainovic was conveying information to Mr. Lukic, which he should not have conveyed, nor should Mr. Lukic have listened to him. Mr. Lukic may have been labouring under an illusion, thinking it really was the case, but Mr. Sainovic was not labouring under any illusion. It all started with Prekaz and Jashari; and of course, yes, Racak took place much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Was the security service monitoring the phones of Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service was monitoring all communications to the extent it was able to technically; as far as I know, Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic because they were prone to conveying Milosevic's private orders even when it was against the interests of Serbia, were subject to operative surveillance to the extent this was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have a whole number of questions arising out of this, but maybe you're still exploring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I would welcome --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, some of them are for you. Have efforts been made to find this tape? Can you help me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, efforts have been made to find a tape of that conversation from a different source, and we have not been able to obtain it. A different source, I mean -- a different source of the intercept, not the SDB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But has an attempt been made to obtain it from the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that there'd been an effort to obtain this specific tape, because it was only in proofing the witness this last weekend that it was indicated to us that he had listened to a copy of the tape that was made by the SDB, as opposed to one that we believed existed from another intercepter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may follow from what you've said that it's also recent news to you that western sources have tapes showing instructions being given by Mr. Sainovic to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That specific part of it regarding instructions to Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if there are such tapes, then clearly some effort ought to have been made to recover these.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were aware of a story in the New York newspaper in January of 1999 about an intercepted conversation involving Mr. Sainovic and at least one of the other accused but not Mr. Lukic. Efforts have been made to determine whether indeed that newspaper account was accurate, whether such a tape had existed, and whether we can get it. We have not been able to get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you seem to have answered at least -- in fact, the main question I had for Mr. Tanic, which I will ask him nevertheless. Where was it you had access to this recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one of the official offices of the State Security Service. We were discussing the problem and they said, "Well, you can hear for yourself what kind of chaos there is down there." I heard parts of the tape, not the entire tape. They have quite a few tapes. To assist the Court and the Prosecutor, I believe they published parts of those tapes on Radio B92 . I know that a few months later I suddenly heard something that sounded familiar, and I thought to myself, "Oh, this is what I heard." And I knew that all the problems originated from this parallel chain of command, and they wanted to draw public attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to confine yourself to the questions I'm asking you because it does lead on to -- that does lead on to other matters, and I will take them up if Mr. Hannis has exhausted in topic. He seems to have assumed in what he said to me that this was a recording of a telephone conversation. Do you know the nature of this recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the usual kind of recording when communications are being intercepted or tapped into. I'm not an expert on the technical issues, and I'm sure I didn't hear the entire tape. I'm sure there is much more material there. This was only to illustrate a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But conversations can be recorded in different circumstances. Do you know whether it was a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. Yes, it was a telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you be any more specific about the content of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult because, initially, it was a general conversation, and then they probably didn't play the whole tape to me. But from the nature of the conversation, it became clear to Sainovic was giving certain instructions to Mr. Lukic about removing corpses, and before that in connection with certain combat activities. I was informed by the service that it was Sainovic and Lukic who were talking. I didn't know Mr. Lukic at the time, so I cannot say from my own knowledge who the voices belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does that apply to both voices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because I have only a superficial private knowledge of Sainovic, so to be fair I do have to say that this applies to both voices. However, it's crucial that parts of the tape were later on broadcast in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What made you conclude that the conversation related to Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Racak was mentioned in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm about to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraphs 54 through 69. In March of 1999, Mr. Tanic, specifically the 22nd and 23rd, one and two days before the NATO bombing started, were you aware of some efforts by Vuk Draskovic to try and come up with a way to prevent the impending NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, first of all, for the Judges, would you tell us who Vuk Draskovic is and what position he had at the time.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was the deputy prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And he is a well-known personality, so there's no need to go into it. He's a well-known public figure. At the time, his official position was that of deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was he --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Interpreter's Correction: He was the vice-president; he was the vice-president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was he trying to do? What proposal did he have to try and prevent the NATO bombing from beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe the interpreters can correct that, because the transcript shows that he was the vice-president of Yugoslavia. Actually, the witness was saying the vice-president of the government of Yugoslavia. And in my understanding, that's a deputy prime minister. But -- so in my opinion the first translation was okay. Now we are having a problem in the transcript because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for the intervention, but I'm sure it can be clarified on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we have a note of it in the transcript that will allow us to make sure that we get the facts on that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, can you tell us what proposal he had in mind, or what was he trying to do to prevent the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the same proposal in mind that Mihajlovic and I had, but we were not in the government. So Mihajlovic asked him to become involved in the whole problem, but Vuk Draskovic would have done so in any case. The essence of the effort was that as we knew that NATO was ready to set foot in Yugoslavia under the auspices of the UN and the Security Council, not as the NATO -- as NATO, but as Milosevic was trying to delude the Yugoslav public, saying that NATO wanted to intervene in Yugoslavia under its own flag, Vuk Draskovic discussed this with Mihajlovic and myself. And he drew up a proposal, which his group of MPs tabled, and that was to accept the presence of NATO units, but under the flag of the UN and with a UN mandate; and to sign the political solution that I've mentioned so many times, which had existed for many years and which ultimately Milosevic agreed on with Holbrooke, and to put this forward at the Assembly session, which was the decisive session before the NATO intervention was to take place or not to take place. There was a whole series of meetings, a number of meetings, with Vuk Draskovic, involving some other people as well. And he discussed this with Milosevic, and Milosevic added on his own initiative only that the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should be respected. And there was some mention of secession. So this was supposed to be adopted by the Assembly. Holbrooke was waiting in Belgrade for the Assembly decision, to see whether he would return to Washington with Serbia's decision for peace or the decision of the Milosevic regime in favour of war. Vuk Draskovic made enormous efforts to prevent the conflict, but I'm not testifying on his behalf. Anyway, that was the essence of the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you indicated that Mr. Milosevic had made one change to the proposal by Mr. Draskovic, having a phrase about respecting the sovereignty of Yugoslavia and Serbia. Was that the only change he had with it at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the only change. Milosevic pretended that it was all all right and even promised to issue instructions to have this adopted at the Assembly session. We all went home happily, expecting that there would be no war, but the next day things turned out differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The proposal suggested by Mr. Draskovic allowed for the possibility in the presence of UN troops to monitor the situation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, under the flag of the UN and with mandate from the Security Council to act as separation forces and even to coordinate with the Pristina Corps, so to keep the Pristina Corps there. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we put up Exhibit P2483, please, and the side-by-side version if possible. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you actually see this document at the time, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I participated in drawing it up, but of course I don't want to take the main credit for it. It's Mihajlovic and Draskovic who should take most of the credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a -- this is a copy that was typed up from the original which had the handwritten change. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I also see the first page, please? Yes, yes. This has refreshed my memory now, and I can clarify what Milosevic added in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, in fairness to you I think we should show you another exhibit. This would be P710. Because as I understand from your statement, there was a typed version made from the original fax because the fax was somewhat illegible.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the proposal from Rambouillet with certain corrections, and Milosevic added, with respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, foreign troops would have to be under the UN flag. Milosevic adopted this because we were also part of the UN troops, I mean, the Yugoslav army. So there would be no obstacle to their arriving under that flag on the territory of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean this is a different document now? When you say this is the proposal from Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you explain that, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a different document. I have just remembered all the points of the document; but in essence, it's advocates signing the Rambouillet agreement, and the presence of foreign troops under the UN flag and with a mandate from the Security Council. It was the presence of foreign troops that was the problem. The political agreement was a problem, to be sure, but not a major problem. It was the modality that was the problem. And later on this formulation was arrived at that had to do with the UN, but as far as I know it was agreed on orally. It's not put down on paper here. There is only a proposal that the Rambouillet agreement be signed and to remove provisions infringing on the sovereignty of the FRY, that is, that foreign troops should arrive under the UN flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the bottom of both pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And paragraph 6 makes reference to that in this draft agreement that was proposed by Mr. Draskovic on the 22nd of March, indicating the Serbs' willingness to sign the agreement or proposed agreement that had been worked out in Rambouillet but never signed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was not Vuk Draskovic's proposal; this was a proposal of all those political leaders in Serbia who were in favour of peace. And Vuk Draskovic, as the deputy prime minister of the FRY, had the strength to put this in the form of a -- an official proposal, rather than private proposal, private suggestion.
