Many people stand behind this proposal; and as regards the other part of the question, yes, the intention was that the Rambouillet agreement should be signed, provided the provisions concerning the third republic be removed. And this was not one of the original requests made at Rambouillet. The apple of discord was actually the arrival of troops which were to be in the peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 of both the English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 2 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the top of each page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us where Mr. Milosevic had made his handwritten amendment, and what it says?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows the part of the sentence where the Security Council is mentioned and the framework of the political agreement, including the guarantee of-- for the agreement. It says with respect for sovereignty and constitution of the FRY, this is Milosevic's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what happened the next day? Was the proposal accepted?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this was a draft of conclusions. Milosevic promised that it would be accepted, but the next day things turned out completely different. Mr. Milutinovic was trying to convince the Assembly, or rather, he consented at the Assembly that the political agreement was not a problem, that we could have had the political agreement. And for the first time after so many years, we were able to hear that this was possible, to reach a favourable political agreement on Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What is said in the Assembly of Republic of Serbia is a matter of public record. It is a political speech and the words speak for themselves. We don't need a fact witness trying to decipher and put an interpretation on them. It's a public record. It's a public speech. Your Honours can read it as well as anyone else. You don't need this witness, who's not qualified to give opinion on anyone's words, to do this in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you think that he has tried to give an opinion about his words? I thought he had departed from that initial indication, and it's equally true, Mr. O'Sullivan, that you can draw his attention to the exact words if you feel that he hasn't accurately reflected them in his evidence. So while noting that you may be right in principle, should an effort be made to put a gloss on words without foundation. So far, I don't see that happening in this evidence and, therefore, that objection is repelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, had you completed your answer?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just to remind myself what I had already said. After acknowledging that the political agreement was not an issue, Milutinovic stated that NATO troops insist and wish to enter the territory of Serbia and Kosovo, exclusively under the auspices or at part of the mandate of the UN forces, but this was simply incorrect. Mr. Milutinovic was simply not saying the truth. For the first time, he acknowledged that the political agreement was not a problem, and Milosevic was quite upset with him afterwards, but then he resumed with the latter part, trying to dispatch wrong information. He mentioned the ultimatum, but he didn't mention the possibility that the Pristina Corps might be allowed to stay and to cooperate with the UN troops in peace implementation. Since he presented this as a military ultimatum, the proposal was rejected, and Holbrooke went home with Serbia's decision to go into war. It was made based on wrong interpretation and wrong information, and Mr. Milutinovic participated in that because it was not correct that NATO insisted on its own flag and its own mandate. It was always under the mandate of the Security Council and the UN flag, plus the Pristina Corps which were allowed to stay in Kosovo, in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and move on to after the NATO bombing started. After that commenced, did you personally get involved or engage in any efforts to reach a peace accord and stop the bombing; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell the Court what you did in connection with that. Did you -- were you allowed to travel outside of Serbia to try and engage in that process?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having in mind my previous numerous contacts I had with them, the State Security Service and Mr. Mihajlovic were most interested to try to come up with a peaceful solution and to bring an end to the war. And they made it possible for me to leave the country, although it was prohibited at the time. I was taken out by one of their employees, and I was given mandate by the security service to try to do something via my personal contacts in the west to try and put an end to the tragedy of our people. Later, I learned that there was another person who was dispatched with the same mission. If you want me to say what exactly I did, then it would require a rather long answer. Of course the security service gave me that mandate with Milosevic's consent, otherwise it would have been out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You started your answer by saying because your previous numerous contacts, you're referring to contacts with western governments or western security services?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western governments and a western security service, and I was actively working on the Kosovo issue for five years. Everyone knew that I was a credible figure in the discussions, both at home and abroad. To be precise, three western governments were in question and one western security service -- intelligence security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this relates to paragraphs 121 to 127 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of your going out to engage in this process, did you -- were you able to receive any sort of proposals or offers which you took back to Serbia and delivered to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received confirmation from two very credible western sources. I was given a precisely defined proposal for a short end to the war, although it was highly secretive. Later on Mr. Lilic received the same, and both plans tally. And I can describe their proposal in detail. It was a western proposal. It stated that NATO would not cease its attacks, but they suggested a gradual suspension of attacks. It also foresaw the simultaneous withdrawal of our forces from Kosovo; and at that time, it was no longer for the Pristina Corps to remain, the Assembly being the last chance for it to remain in Kosovo. Therefore, our troops were to withdraw from Kosovo simultaneously with the NATO bombing suspension. The initial period was for 24 hours and, provided the withdrawal continued, it would be prolonged for another 24 hours, then 48, and then until complete cessation. So what was discussed was a gradual decrease in the frequency of bombing and not its complete stop. And now we have the Holbrooke agreement that everyone can recall, which came into place immediately as soon as bombs started showering the country. And it included various countries like the US, Italy, Germany, and so on and so forth, especially the G8 was involved; and that would have meant the end of the war. That was in March -- well, late March/early April. I know it for a fact, since my birthday is in early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When -- you say this was conveyed to Mr. Milosevic. How was that conveyed to him? Did you do that personally or through a third party?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This came from the highest western source, or rather, two highest western sources, and through official state security channels I forwarded that information, and then it was forwarded to Milosevic. Later I found out that at the same time, he offered the same proposal via Lilic through the German and Austrian channels; and of course in the meantime, I informed Mihajlovic, who also conveyed that to Milosevic. I for my part conveyed that Mr. Milutinovic, and so on and so forth. In any case, Milosevic knew right away and he knew what my mission was, otherwise they wouldn't have let me leave the country and talk to foreign players. These foreign people would not have talked to me without Milosevic's consent. At the time it was ultra secret and it was nowhere to be found in the public domain. It was also secret when I explained that to the ICTY; therefore, in late March 1999, NATO was willing to cease its attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the transcript you've been translated as saying that you forwarded it through official state security channels to Milosevic. "Later I found out that at the same time he offered the same proposal via Lilic through the German and Austrian channels." Now, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't offer, but he received the same proposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Milosevic's response was to this offer that you had forwarded through state security channels, and the similar or same offer that had been received by him from Mr. Lilic. Do you know what he replied?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In my case he said, "Delay, delay, go again. Check. See if they're lying." It was completely irrational. Later I learned that Lilic went through the same thing, although he was much closer to him. Again, I went abroad at a later stage, and the response was in any case negative. Milosevic did not accept the proposal, but rather, he opted for the prolongation of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that regard, did you have - now I'm talking to paragraphs 108 and 117 and 118 - during the course of the NATO bombing, did you personally have any conversation with Mr. Milosevic about the bombing and about civilian casualties, Serb civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a brief conversation. I cannot be specific as to its detail, but I remember him saying that we needed civilian casualties to justify everything. He's dead now, but there were some other people who were present. It is a state secret, and it is up to this Tribunal to assess the truthfulness of everything I say. Milosevic, in any case, simply said that there had to be civilian casualties among the Serbs to justify the whole thing. He simply was unable to accept NATO's peace proposal or truce, and NATO was offered to extend their hand to him. It was during the war and after the war as well, and it's a terrible tragedy for the people which took place because Milosevic and his friends, and it was certainly a terrible tragedy for the Kosovar Albanians. Both parties will suffer for a long time to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow up on that. You say he said there had to be civilian casualties among the Serbs to justify the whole thing. Can you explain what he meant about that, if you know; or did he explain? I don't understand the sense of that. How would that justify the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to show that the NATO pact are criminals, animals. He had a whole list of NATO targets, and he could have evacuated the civilians and, nonetheless, he didn't. He knew about the RTS, the radio-television Serbia, for three or four days before it was bombed. I told him that, as well as some other people, but he didn't evacuate the personnel, rather, he evacuated or took out all the furniture from the building owned by his daughter. He simply allowed to Serb casualties happen, and he wanted to picture to show that NATO was the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing I've been saying all day: What is this? Talk, talk, one story, another story. I don't understand. What furniture? That was not a response to the question. I don't think this should go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was by way of illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, there's a decision to be made on an objection taken. I think part of the problem here is there's a part omitted from that last answer, and it was, to my mind, if I heard it properly the most directly relevant part of it. You said, Mr. Tanic, he knew -- it says he knew from the RTS, the Radio Television Serbia, three or four days before it was bombed. I think you were saying that he knew that it was going to be bombed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, four days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You then went on to say something about your own involvement. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four days before the RTS building was to be bombed, I was abroad and I was told by our friends - we had a lot of friends abroad who could distinguish between Serbia and Milosevic's regime - via secure telephone communication -- well, first I was told that this was going to happen; and then via secure telephone conversation, I conveyed this to Belgrade. Later on I learned that there was such information coming from other sources as well. The RTS was not evacuated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Mr. Fila, that's a statement that a witness of direct involvement in a chain of events which he claims might have led to the building being evacuated before it was bombed. That seems, to me, to be relevant and to be a matter also of which he has some personal knowledge and not simply material similar to that to which you have objected earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not trying to distinguish between the important and unimportant parts. I'm trying to say this: The witness is to answer Mr. Hannis's question. And Mr. Hannis surely would have eventually come up with this question, but the witness just goes on and on. And then we have the issue of the transcript, something is military secret, something is state secret, someone told him something, we don't know who. What's he got to do with any state secrets? It is something for civil servants. And if something was a state secret, why couldn't he reveal the source. So my objection is in principle to the way he provides his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we note your comments. Mr. Hannis knows perfectly well that unattributed information is unlikely to be of any significance to the mind of the Trial Chamber and has been asking for further details where things are said that seem to him to be of some importance. Mr. Tanic, it is -- it will remain helpful to us if you can try to confine the answers you give to the particular question that's asked. The more specifically answered, the more valuable for our purposes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to the RTS event that you told us about, did the SDB, security service, also receive information about other future targets of NATO bombing? Just yes or no, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they pass that information on to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to imagine that they didn't. I didn't see anything -- any information being directly given or passed on to Milosevic, but it is difficult for me to imagine that they wouldn't do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would have been their obligation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was their obligation, and many honest people still work there after -- particularly after Stanisic's removal; the same goes for the army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to paragraph 123 of your statement. Were you aware of an effort in late March or early April 1999 by the Vatican to try and help settle the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I was involved in discussions with them as well as the Vatican Foreign Minister, Angelo Sodano, who came with the same peace message to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that proposal incountenance a cease-fire or a temporary cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A unilateral cease-fire and the beginning of withdrawal of our forces. On the other hand, the frequency of bombing was supposed to decrease. The unilateral cease-fire was to happen during the Catholic Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "unilateral cease-fire," which side was supposed to cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side, the Yugoslav side. That was stop with any combat activities and was supposed to start withdrawing. At the same time NATO was supposed to suspend bombing, so as to create the preconditions for KFOR insertion and their troops were already at the borders. I wish to point out that I wasn't able to read any of that prior to my conveying them to The Hague Tribunal; therefore, I couldn't have known in any other way, apart from being included in the whole story. And I would kindly ask the Defence counsel not to insult me any further by saying that I learned something from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, let me ask you: You say this was supposed to happen during the Catholic Easter. Do you know, had Mr. Milosevic initially accepted this proposal and agreed to implement a cease-fire starting on Catholic Easter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He pretended he was overwhelmed. He would promise anything but never did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did the cease-fire happen on Catholic Easter, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When it failed to happen, did you do anything to try to find out about why it had not been implemented on that day?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, and the president of my party, Mihajlovic, as well as some other people. Just to say something regarding the last answer, there were also offers made to release the captured soldiers as part of that proposal. We took everything -- we made every effort we could, including Draskovic and Lilic and many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which captured soldiers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess there were two or three captured American pilots at the time. I just wanted to clarify things further because this could appear tomorrow in some text, and then they will say, "Well, you see Mr. Tanic has got no clue."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did you contact to try and find out why the cease-fire had not gone through on Catholic Easter, as you thought it was going to?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service, Milosevic himself; Mihajlovic contacted Milutinovic, and I suppose Milosevic as well. Perhaps we could refresh my memory, because it was at the time when I was trying to save my own head, my own hide. It was a risky game for me to play, as well as for some other people. Perhaps I could be allowed to consult my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before we resort to that, let me ask you: Did you, with Mr. Mihajlovic, participate in a conversation with anyone about why it had not gone through as proposed?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we found Milutinovic from the cabinet at one of the command posts. Of course, it wasn't easy, one couldn't talk normally, and then there was this conversation with Milutinovic as to why this had not been implemented. Milutinovic replied that there was still some unfinished business down there, and that it would happen on Orthodox Easter. In my opinion, we had no business down there, except for more crimes to be committed, traces to be removed, and our people to be killed for no reason, because there was intensive bombing at the time and nothing could be done in the military sense, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this a face-to-face conversation or a phone conversation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was through means of communication. I told you that Milutinovic was at a command post. I don't know whether Mihajlovic and Milutinovic met up later on. As far as Mihajlovic told me, he did have more meetings, including face-to-face meetings, but I did not attend these. Mihajlovic confirmed to me, of course, that he had more meetings, but I don't want to engage in conveying hearsay. There was a telephone conversation. Mr. Milutinovic was at one of the secret command posts, and we from the cabinet had a hard time finding him. Draskovic was looking for Bulatovic. Well, the situation was quite chaotic, as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That raises a number of questions as well for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're pursuing it, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer. You mentioned Milutinovic replying that there was still some unfinished business down there. This was a conversation with Milutinovic. Who -- first of all, who participated in that conversation with Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihajlovic, and I was able to listen in through the means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the means of communication was, was it a telephone or a radio?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a special telephone, as far as I can remember. I'm no technology expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the only part I wanted to follow-on. Was there other parts you wanted to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was a reference there to the cabinet. You said that, "we from the cabinet had a hard time finding him." What do you mean by the reference there to the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, Mihajlovic's office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: That it's the same word in B/C/S: "Cabinet" can also mean office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of his office and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just the impression could have been created that this was -- he was still holding a government position, but by this time Mihajlovic is not part of the government. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to paragraphs 143 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, as a result of your relationship with the SDB, did you have any knowledge about Mr. Milosevic's control, if any, over the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had complete control, both in Mr. Stanisic's time and later in Mr. Rade Markovic's time, but they were two different services. When Rade Markovic became the chief, it was no longer the same security service as it had been in Mr. Stanisic's time. But in both cases, Mr. Milosevic had complete control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, now I don't understand your question. We knew each other for so many years. Are you looking for a specific piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'll start with a question about the chain of command within the State Security Service. Who was the head of the State Security Service in 1998? You've told us before.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have. After Mr. Stanisic was replaced, Radomir Markovic was placed at its head. He was a man from the public security who had never worked in intelligence before; then Uros Suvakovic, one of the ideologues of the SBS, who knew nothing about intelligence work, and he was the main controllers of the service. Uros Suvakovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the immediate superior or boss of Mr. Stanisic and then later Markovic, would that be the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes. But in Serbia in practice, this was never respected. Formally and legally, yes, Vlajko Stojiljkovic was his superior, but you can't imagine Stanisic or Rade Markovic respecting what he had to say. De facto, Milosevic was the superior; de jure, it was the Minister of Police or the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what position Mr. Stojiljkovic held before he became Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew him quite well. He had been the president of the chamber of economy; and in that capacity, we had discussed certain business ventures. He was a businessman, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the organisational structure or the Government of Serbia and Yugoslavia, what -- who was the boss of the Minister of the Interior? Who selected the Minister of the Interior, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior is appointed, not elected. I know that there's a difference between the English and the Serbian here. And it should be the Serbian government, as far as I am familiar with the law, but this was never respected and nobody paid much attention to it down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, I want to move forward to the time when you left Serbia. Can you briefly tell the Judges how it came about that you left Serbia and became a protected witness living in another country.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, around the middle or right after the capitulation of Kumanovo, as it was clear to me, I started preparing a book about the conflicts in Kosovo entitled, "The Kosovo Inflict: A Fabricated War." I said it was a fabricated war because I was sure that Milosevic and his associates had fabricated it. But to check what I wanted to write about and the book was to include the things we've discussed and some other things, in order to verify all this because these are all serious accusations and parts of those accusations might look like science fiction, I as an educated man and an intellectual was aware of that, I started talking to relevant people in order to double-check my conclusions, to make sure that I was not mistaken about something, and to make sure that I had not been so hard hit by the tragedy that I was unable to see clearly. So I started talking to the State Security Service, asking to gain access to the documentation, the archives on victims on both sides. I asked to talk to Perisic, to check his military viewpoints, to see whether they coincided with my political and intelligence information. I went to Rome to meet with Monsignor Paglia, who spoke on behalf of the contact group. I wanted to double-check to hear again what Milosevic had said to him. In the meantime, he had become a bishop. I told him what I wanted to check, and we talked. I talked to a number of ambassadors and so on. And just before my last conversation with Perisic, the day before the attempted assassination of Vuk Draskovic on the Ibarska main road, I was kidnapped in the street, I was abducted. Of course, I saw that the road was blocked, but by the time I saw that it was too late. They attacked me. They grabbed me. They pushed me into a van. They injected me with something to make me go to sleep; then my wife was kidnapped. Later on we found out these were JSO units, units for special operations, and we were tortured in a private prison for a day and a half. It was not a legal prison. We were interrogated. I was asked why I was preparing material for this book? Did I know what this meant? What did the British have to do with it, as if they had heard about it for the first time, although they had had contacts with them through me. Then whether Perisic wanted to conduct a coup d'etat with Stanisic. It was kind of a Latin American [Realtime transcript read in error "Latin"] Torture that I was subjected to. They tried to make me confess so that Perisic and Stanisic had wanted to implement a coup d'etat against Milosevic; and various other matters. And I was quite certain that they were getting ready to murder me because Curuvija had been liquidated in a similar way, and I knew how this unit operated. Suddenly, they released is, both my wife and me. She had been kidnapped two hours lather than after me. And later on I learned that this had taken place a few hours after the unsuccessful attempt to assassinate Vuk Draskovic on the Ibarska main road. So seeing that they were murdering people - and this is a very important matter - I must explain the reasons why I left the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is speaking way too rapidly for the translators to keep up, I'm convinced. If you look at lines 64 -- page 64, line 3, what he said was not that it was a Latin torture but that it was an American torture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A Latin American torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, a Latin American. In any event, I think he needs to slow down rapidly, because we're not getting a transcript as to what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, normally we get a message to that effect, but, in case you are right, I will ask Mr. Tanic to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, if you could continue, and I understand this was important and significant in your life, but can you be as concise as possible and tell me how you came to leave after being kidnapped and tortured, and what happened after you were released.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I was released, I came to understand that this had been done by a JSO unit, and that our release was a pure stroke of luck, because the attempt on Vuk Draskovic's life had not been successful and they wanted to play a game of theirs. I won't go into details. And a few days later, I realised my wife and I had been put into what is colloquially referred to as a cage. That means round-the-clock surveillance. My wife, for example, travelled to Bar, which is a town on the Montenegrin coast, to sell a piece of property there. They followed her. She was able to see that. We couldn't drink a coke together in peace. This is what they referred to as a cage. Something like that had been done in the case of Mr. Curuvija, who was already unfortunately deceased. And I came to understand that my life was under a serious threat. They knew about the book, about the information I was gathering, and I had already been cooperating with The Hague Tribunal. Maybe they had information about that, although they never asked me about that, I have to say. They never mentioned it. So I simply left the country in order to save my life. I used the pretext which sounded acceptable. I took just two suitcases and 200 German marks, which amounts to a hundred euros in today's money, because anything else would have been suspicious. I want to say I'm referring to the torture in colloquial terms because I don't want to evince pity from you, but my wife and I were beaten, throttled, she was stripped naked. They threatened to rape her. They made me listen to her scream; then they could come to me and say: "We are going to rape your wife. We're going to kill her, unless you admit that Perisic and Stanisic, together with Jovic, wanted to implement a coup d'etat. Why are you writing this book? What gives you the right to say these things? Milosevic is not a traitor." So there was total chaos and I saw that Mr. Milosevic, through his channels, had given them some misinformation, but this was certainly a JSO unit. My kidnapping by the JSO is confirmed in a book written by Mr. Mijatovic, the deputy chief of the State Security Service. He described the circumstances differently, but he did admit that my wife and I were kidnapped by the JSO. And under Rade Markovic, it was a death squad. Later on, it liquidated many people or attempted to liquidate them, as you may know. And because I knew this and because for many years I what had been close, not to that unit, but closely involved with those problems, I left the country in order to save my life; otherwise, I would have been killed, as some people were later on, or I would have ended up in prison, although I was innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after leaving the country, without going into details, is it fair to say that you received some assistance from some of the western security services that you had dealt with, you eventually testified in the Milosevic case, and you were relocated to a third country. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was immediately received by the Hungarian government and by western intelligence agency, which unfortunately has already been mentioned -- well, with the agreement of that agency, I was received and it was made possible for us to recover physically. We were in a terrible state. These people knew me from before. They knew I was telling the truth. I was not received in order for me to testify, but in order for my and my wife's lives to be saved. But I testified because I am convinced that everything I have to say is true and that Milosevic's regime, a handful of people, created a tragedy, both for the Serbs and for the Albanians in Kosovo. And that this amounted to treachery, to betrayal of their own country. They knew, because I did not conceal my standpoint in Belgrade. I spoke out about this. I spoke in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I have just clarification of one expression you used at the very beginning of this passage of evidence, "the capitulation of Kumanova."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead. What kind of clarification, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After he rejected all the peace proposals, he signed the capitulation of Kumanovo; because in the meantime, the Hague Tribunal had brought an indictment against him, and he knew the NATO troops would be coming to get him. He signed the Kumanovo capitulation; it was not peace. It was a capitulation compared to the solutions we have had before. Any expert can show this. It is called the Kumanovo agreement, which put an end to the bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, two final matters I wanted to deal with. Once -- when you testified during Milosevic, Mr. Milosevic made suggestions that you were a political nobody and that you couldn't have possibly been in the position you claim to be in, to have seen and done the things you claimed. I would like to show you Exhibit P522 at this time. There are some photographs I would like you to take a look at, and if you could help us tell the Court who is in these photographs. In the top photograph, can you tell us who's there, the ones that you recognise. And if you could point or indicate whether you're starting on the left or the right or whatever.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first this is Mr. Milosevic's office when he was still the president of Serbia. This was a regular annual meeting between the coalition parties. Mr. Milosevic is in the middle, to the far right is myself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite clear this is an official meeting of the delegation of New Democracy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please, Mr. Tanic. There was just an issue of directing your voice into the microphone, please, Mr. Tanic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am on the far right wearing glasses. I see now that I'm the only one wearing glasses in the picture. Next to me is one of Mr. Mihajlovic's advisors, Mr. Goran Karadjole; and then the deputy prime minister, Ceda Mirkovic, from the party of New Democracy; and then Mr. Mihajlovic standing next to Mr. Milosevic, the late Mr. Milosevic; behind him is Radulovic; and then behind is the chef de cabinet of Mr. Mihajlovic, Ivan Djordjevic; then two ladies. I have forgotten their names, unfortunately, as I did not use politics to deepen personal friendships. Then there is also Zagorac on the far left. So this is the Executive Committee of New Democracy and two advisors of Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before we go any further with this, bear in mind that these may be visible at the moment, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but these have been published before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not outside -- only in the courtroom. Yes. I was just concerned that they were visible outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had discussed this with the witness before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He felt comfortable with that. But if they're not going outside the courtroom, that's even better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this exhibit would be admitted under seal then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would be our request, Your Honour. Can we scroll down to the bottom photograph on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First, that photograph on the left, can you tell us who's in that from left to right.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milutinovic's cabinet, when he was the Minister of Foreign Affairs. I am to the far left. Then behind, Mr. Goran Karadjole; then Mr. Mihajlovic; Mr. Milutinovic in the middle; and Cedo Mirkovic. This was a working meeting. You can see that we are in quite a good mood, not because we'd had a drink but because we'd exchanged opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately when was that picture taken, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall precisely, really, but you have photo documentation about New Democracy, as much as you like. I think this was when we had our first official meeting with Mr. Milutinovic. Mr. Mihajlovic held him in high regard, as did I, because he was an experienced diplomat. We were trying to have serious working contacts with Mr. Milutinovic, who was working on similar issues as Mr. Mihajlovic and I, simply to join forces for the benefit of the country, because we knew that Mr. Milutinovic knew all those things, and the fact that he followed Milosevic doesn't mean that he was not an experienced and clever man. I hold him in high regard. To the right, you can see me with the Italian ambassador, Mr. Ricardo Sosa. This photograph is important because Mr. Sosa, at that time, was the only remaining ambassador from the NATO countries while NATO was bombing. He stayed in Belgrade, and as such was one of the channels for secret negotiations. He held meetings with Draskovic, with me, certainly with Milutinovic, and others. He can also confirm certain things that have to do with the peace proposals of NATO, problems in connection with the Rambouillet political agreement. He was one of the people who was very actively involved in solving the problem. He's an important person, and Milutinovic had a very good opinion of him. He was very pleased that Italian diplomacy had appointed Ricardo Sosa as the ambassador to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the last question I have about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only have one other question I want to cover with the witness, but I would like to go into private session for a minute to discuss something related to that. I don't know if you want to do that right now or when we come back from the break, because we go into closed session to take him in and out of the room anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, let's do it now and that will bring your examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, is it correct that in 1977 you were convicted of a crime in the district court in Belgrade, for which you received a term of imprisonment or incarceration for a year and two months, which, on appeal, was reduced to seven months and for which you actually served six months of time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was convicted to serve seven months. The first judgement was irrelevant because it was quashed by the supreme court. I was to serve seven months in prison, with the recommendation that I be released after five or six, because it was an offence which had not been committed but there was suspicion that I may have committed. It refers to something which took place in 1976, that is, 30 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this document has been identified as 1D030565, I believe. In the English, it describes the crime as looting, but I know in informal discussions with one of my language assistants, I'm told it could be robbery or it could be burglary, so I'm not clear on what the exact offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In referring to this as 1D, are you saying that it is an exhibit for the first accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The number can't possibly be 30.565, at least I hope it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm reading the number on the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's our ERN equivalent, Your Honour, page number as opposed to document number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll settle for 1D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into closed session -- sorry, yes, we will go into closed session just now while the witness leaves, and we'll remain that way until he returns.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have the order. I'll be first, then Mr. Sainovic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, General Lukic, and General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you know Veton Surroi, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know that he's a respected newspaper editor and an intellectual?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also a political figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecution, you state that you met Mr. Surroi in 1989, you met him many times, and you are his friend. And my question is: What's your impression of him? Is he a decent man, an honest man? What can you say?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I knew him, he was an intelligent and honest person, but of course he represented the Albanian position. I cannot tell you what he's like today, because I haven't seen him for at least seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: P2361 is the OTP interview with Veton Surroi, and it's admitted into evidence, and I'm quoting from page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, on page 9 of his statement is talking about the Bertelsmann Foundation meeting in Rhodos in September 1996, which both you and Mr. Surroi attended. Now, Mr. Tanic, Mr. Surroi testified in this trial and his evidence is the following: "Ratomir Tanic, an advisor to Mihajlovic, was also involved. Tanic said that he had direct contact to Milosevic, but I didn't believe him. I have a personal history of mistrust with Tanic."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, why do you think Mr. Surroi said that about you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that question should be posed to Mr. Surroi and not to me. I don't know what's in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Didn't he say that because you have a history of not telling the truth and being dishonest?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for him to speculate what was in Mr. Surroi's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. I'm asking Mr. Tanic whether he has a history of being dishonest and untrustworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan, the question is admissible, but the answer is unlikely to assist us. However, please answer the question, Mr. Tanic. Put in a slightly different form. The question is: Do you have a history of being dishonest and untrustworthy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were it listen to gossip, then yes; but if you were to go by facts, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were born on the 6th of April, 1966, and you're the son of Lazar, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In translation, or rather, in the transcript, I see 1966; whereas, it should be 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps, I misspoke. It should have been 1956. And did you live in Belgrade all your adult life until you left in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have a question about your education, and I'm talking about the period when you were still living in Serbia until 1999. When you testified in the Milosevic trial, you said that you had completed elementary school and that you were literate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since he kept insisting on my educational background; however, I did not feel to -- obliged to illustrate by educational background since I wasn't there as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it's correct that you have elementary school and you're literate. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but I've also completed another couple of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, again in the Milosevic trial, and this is Exhibit 1D27, the 15th of May, 2002, page 5027, you were asked this question: "Right. So what you're saying is your education level is a secondary education level. Is that it? A gymnasium?" "A. No. I did not complete a gymnasium, a secondary school. "Q. What school do you have then? "A. Secondary economic school. "Q. All right. So secondary economics. School of economics. Is that it? "A. No, that's not what I said. We would have to call in experts here to ascertain the level of education. I don't wish to answer questions that have nothing to do with this trial." All you admitted to, sir, is that you have an elementary school education. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. And later I stated that I have a high school degree in economics, a diploma.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Last week when you testified, you said that in the mid-1970s to early 1990s, by occupation you worked as a tradesman in some sort of federal institution. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What was your trade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean by profession or by education? By education, I'm a master of political science; as regards profession, I cannot tell you. Because as part of the witness protection programme, I was forced to do some common jobs. I studied several -- at several schools. I have university degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are being asked about the situation prior to your involvement in that scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the mid-1970s to the early 1990s. Maybe I can help focus you. That's the period I'm interested in. You told the Prosecutor that between the mid-1970s to the early 1990s you worked as a tradesman in some federal institution. And I'm asking as a tradesman, what was your trade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had a high school degree as a -- as technical staff for economics, and I had begun studying other courses. At the time, when I was examined by Milosevic, I wasn't willing to discuss that with him. But I will answer any of your questions, if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Please answer. What was your trade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I replied. A technical assistant or technical staff in economics; that's what we called it in Serbia. Any person having a high school diploma in Serbia, in economics, carried that title.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And which federal institution did you work in?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a business association of the dairy factories in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So if you were a technician, why in the Milosevic trial did you introduce yourself as a businessman?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I became a businessman, since I started producing goods abroad. After that, I was a small-scale industrialist, and I didn't work with that institution in early 1980s, but rather until the end of the 1980s. That's why I introduced myself as a businessman.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you have a company?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One company or more?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter for this Court, because, first and foremost, we were producing goods. At first, we produced goods as part of a foreign company, and later my partner and myself established some other companies as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did you have one or more companies? What's the answer?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that during my business career there were two companies, of which I was either one of the owners or a full owner. I didn't pay much attention to that because I conducted business to provide for my family. I didn't see that as a career.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So your testimony is you had two companies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, this must be a matter that is simple to answer in a straightforward way. The answers you've given so far leave me very confused about what your activities were. Please bear in mind that the reliability of the material you've given to the Tribunal is a big issue in the case and therefore your general reliability as a witness is something that will be exposed to scrutiny. So it's important to answer the questions in as straightforward a manner as possible; that's the way to assist us to the fullest advantage. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D27 is the Milosevic transcript of 15 May 2002, and on page 5028, Mr. Tanic, you said you had three companies. Why did you say you had three if you only had two?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because one of the companies was labelled by Milosevic as a publishing house; in fact, it wasn't, and I was one of the owners only. And I can't say I owned or had that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. So you owned two companies and you had association with a third; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you choose one of the three. You tell me the name of one of those companies.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was called Evropa Press. That was the one that Milosevic labelled a publishing house. Another company --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, that's fine -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have another question about Evropa Press. When was it established? What year?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I think in 1996/1997. I think 1997 or maybe even somewhat later; however, in that period. It wasn't in 1996, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what was the official seat of that company? What's the street address and number?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the centre of town. I forget the name of the street. It was a very steep street, close to Zeleni Venac, on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're telling me you don't know the street where this company was located in the city in which you grew up?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot the name of the street. I haven't been living in that city for eight years now; however, that street takes you from Terazije downhill to the Zeleni Venac market.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Was that company dissolved; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dissolved after some three to four months -- no, six months at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you say you had two companies. Give me the name of one of the companies that you owned.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One company was called Djils [phoen]. It was a branch of a foreign company. We produced cosmetics with the assistance of a company in Italy, and then the Djils company began producing in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were the owner of that company?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And where was it located in Belgrade? What street? Which number?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was at the same address where Evropa Press was -- well, we had some partner arrangements concerning rent, and I wanted to assist the other company, Evropa Press, as regards the rent they had to pay for the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Was this company dissolved; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after some theft and some outside problems, it simply ceased to exist. And by that time, I was no longer interested in it anyhow. Therefore, yes, it was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I simply can't recall. I'm not trying to avoid your answer. It was a short-lived company of a year or a year and a half. I think it was -- well, I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the second company you owned, what was it called?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in that other company, I wasn't the owner. I was one of the founders, and it was called Finestetik.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when was it founded?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1988 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Has it been dissolved; and if, so when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after one of the employees engaged in stealing and after a criminal report was submitted, by founders' decision, the company ceased to exist and its property was handed over to the principal founder.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And where was its seat? Which street address did it have?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what used to be the 7th of July Street. It's close to a pizzeria. I don't know its current name.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask the usher to distribute materials to the Chamber, the Prosecution, and to Mr. Tanic. The names appear on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you talked about your -- Mr. Tanic, you talked about your --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- your criminal conviction in 1977.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What was that conviction for?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was interpreted as an attempt to commit an offence, since it never actually was. As far as I can recall, it was an attempted theft, as they termed it. It was quashed 25 years ago, and I believe you should know that it carries no weight anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D40 is in hard copy at tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Turn to tab 10, Mr. Tanic. Under tab 10 there are two documents, one in English, one in B/C/S. It's the SFRY Criminal Code of 1973. Mr. Tanic, if you prefer to follow in your language, it's the second page in the B/C/S document, and you see article 16. Do you see that, at tab 10? In front of you, you have documents.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can you turn to tab 10.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes,, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you see the -- the second page of the Serbian, which is actually page 7 of -- in the bottom right-hand corner. You see that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you see Article 16, Sanctions of Attempting Crimes. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms that the crime was attempted, not committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And turn the page, please, and look at Article 255. Do you see Article 255?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's a grave offence; it's theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. Of an amount of over 30.000 dinars, correct, shall be punished by a minimum of five years in prison. Do you see that? Article 255 (1)?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it, but I was punished to serve seven months. It was quashed, annulled, 25 years ago. You are talking about a non-existing judgement, and you know what you are trying to do here is a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Listen to the request questions and answer them. Please treat us as having a modicum of intelligence and an ability to sort out what's valuable and what's invaluable in the criticisms that may be made of your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And can you turn the page once more and see Article 258, it says "fraud."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Theft, fraud, and the rest, but you don't get seven months in Serbia for that. It says here, I should have been given five years. I received seven months, sir. I certainly did not commit theft which foresees the prison sentence of five years, and I was given seven months. This confirms I didn't commit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you're clearly not reading the whole thing. It's not for you to interpret this to us at the moment. It does not say for the charge for attempting to commit theft you get five years, if you will read the thing properly. Now, let's move on, Mr. O'Sullivan. And let's keep your comments to the questions you're being asked, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One last thing, turn to the next page, please. Article 306, do you see that? It says, "Falsifying Official Documents."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go back. Go to tab 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in e-court that is 1D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's the certificate that Mr. Hannis showed you, and you should have both the Serbian and English under tab 1. You'll see that the crime described in the Serbian is "pljacke," which is spelled p-l-j-a-c-k-e with the proper declension. And "pljacke" is theft, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Theft and robbery shouldn't be the same thing. Robbery is worse than theft. "Pljacke" is robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the certificate - and I won't ask you to comment on it - but you see that you were convicted under the articles we looked at together, 255, 258, 306. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D31, that's at tab 2 of your hard copy. There is an English and a Serbian document. What you have there, Mr. Tanic, is the record sheet from your political party, New Democracy. At page 5126 of the Milosevic transcript you said: "This is a photocopy of my admission paper. The signature corresponds to mine, but not -- but the status not." Now, with Mr. Milosevic, you contested the fact that you were simply a supporter of New Democracy. Is that right? Do you recall saying that to Mr. Milosevic? You challenged the status. You said you were not simply a supporter. That's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This sheet is counterfeit.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you adopted it in the Milosevic case. You recognised it. And my question is: Why did you put down that you had a university degree when you didn't?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't put that there. I said that the document is a forgery. My signature -- well, the signature looks like mine, but simply the whole document is a forgery. I did not adopt this document. I asked the Defence not to put words into my mouth, which I never uttered. Besides, everybody knows I was not a sympathiser of New Democracy but a member of the inner leadership, and that I collaborated closely with Mr. Mihajlovic. Newspapers reported on it. I was not a sympathiser. I gave interviews about New Democracy on television; and in the media, I was an advisor. I never wrote that I had graduated from university, although of course my education was very broad. At that time I had a very broad university education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did you or did you not put on the form that you had a university degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I don't use block capitals to make these entries. I hardly ever use capitals like that. I even have difficulty in writing capital letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you also saying that the name you put on the form was not -- the name that appears on the form was not written by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The name and the telephone number, it's just routine, but then things have been added. Pale, I was never registered in that municipality; I never lived there. Later on there's a circle put around sympathiser; things have been added, such as the university. That's why it's a forgery. It says I was registered in Pale municipality, and I never lived there. I did put down my name, address, and telephone number, because those are just routine matters. You put those down so people will know your address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it is also your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably it looks very much like my signature, so I could accept that it's mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We may need the assistance of the usher here to have a copy of Mr. Tanic's witness statement in both English and B/C/S put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We may refer to those documents in due course, sir. Last week, when you testified, you were asked in relation to that statement, which is P2480, about paragraphs 4 and 5, and I will read those to you very quickly and then ask you questions about that. Paragraph 4 - that's on page 2, for your reference - says: "As a member of the ND party and Special Advisor to Dusan Mihajlovic, the President of ND, on international relations in Kosovo, I was chosen to conduct discreet negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians. I received this authorisation directly from Milosevic, in a meeting that I and Dusan Mihajlovic held with him in approximately 1995. I believe I was selected for this position because I had good contacts and relationships with Kosovo Albanian representatives ..."

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what page is this on in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are the Serbian paragraphs numbered the same way, Mr. O'Sullivan? Because if they are, it's paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's not -- Mr. Tanic does not have the numbered paragraphs, but it's page 3 in Serbian, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a numbered version in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. That would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I see it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will help you, though, to also have beside you the copy that the usher has, because it has paragraph numbers, in case any further paragraphs are referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll just finish this paragraph. You say: "I believe I was selected for this position because I had good contacts and relationships with Kosovo Albanian representatives and with international representatives, and was accepted by the SDB from the security perspective. In summary, my political authorisation to conduct these negotiations came from three sources: Milosevic, the SDB, and my party, because it was officially part of the government. The Republic of Serbia government was never consulted on these negotiations." And the first sentence of the next paragraph is: "I was the principal negotiator in these discreet negotiations." Now, I've given you the B/C/S version. Do you have paragraph 5 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've seen this statement. The part where it describes why I was selected is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm referring you to paragraph 5. Do you see paragraph 5, yes or no, in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Could you slowly read the first sentence outloud in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was the chief negotiator in these discreet negotiations." Am I to be held responsible for translation problems? I explained this formulation in great detail during my testimony. Together with the president of my party, I was the most successful negotiator --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me re-read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you obviously want to swap seats with me. Well, that's not going to happen. Just please answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, last week --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation is incorrect. That's my response. The translation does not correspond to the spirit of the Serbian language. It appears that I said I was the chief negotiator and that I'm lying. I'm not responsible for mistranslations which change the meaning of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But your explanation last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Just a moment, Mr. O'Sullivan. I don't understand that comment. You've read it -- this is the reason why you were asked to read it in your own language, so that it would be translated precisely as you read it here, to remove any problems about translation. But the way you read it was identical to what is translated into English in the written version that we have. So what is the point you're trying to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is one slight difference, Your Honour. I think it's been translated here as "chief negotiator" and in the written English it's "principal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say there's a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, they aren't precisely the same words. I don't think there's a difference in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this happens constantly in translation. There's more than one word in different languages for a concept or an expression, and you inevitably get a different one when it's read. But the meaning, the literal meaning, of that translation -- of the two translations is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, perhaps if you focused on the document I want you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like an answer to my question before you get involved again, Mr. O'Sullivan. I would like to know what it is the witness is saying is misleading about the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said that I was the chief negotiator in a formal sense; that would have been fantasy on my part. And it can be checked in a matter of minutes. I never said that formally I was the chief negotiator. I said I was the best negotiator who achieved the most results, which is true. I never said that I was the main or chief negotiator; that would have been a fantasy on my part. And the Defence is constantly trying to impute various fantasies to me. Everybody knows that the chief negotiator was Slobodan Milosevic and Ratko Markovic on his behalf. I'm not a crazy person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you signed the statement in a pseudonym thus, on the face of it, approving the way in which it was recorded, and we now know that the English language used expresses accurately the term used in the Serb language for the same point. You've already explained to us that you regarded yourself as the most successful of the negotiators, along with Mihajlovic. You acknowledge that there were five or six others involved. We've heard all this evidence already. You've had a full opportunity to explain. In cross-examination, it's open to counsel to ask you questions following their approach, and it would serve you well to concentrate on these questions and answer them, to the best of your ability. What you did in the approach you've just taken has caused confusion by suggesting there was a mistranslation into English, when, in fact, what you're saying is that you approved an inaccurate expression of what you meant to say in your own language. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look a little more closely at the situation, Mr. Tanic. The statement, the statement that you signed with the pseudonym, that statement was given by you in English, wasn't it? Look at the cover page. "Language used in interview: English." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on the 4th and 5th of November of this year, you sat down with the Prosecutor here in The Hague and you reviewed this statement, with the addition of a Serbian translation of it, and you made no additions or corrections to the sentence: "I was the principal negotiator in these discreet negotiations." You made no changes, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did draw the Prosecutor's attention to this and the Prosecutor can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Who did you tell that to?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew Mr. Hannis's attention to the fact that there might be some confusion about who was the principal one and who was not, and that in the Serbian language you can say that someone is the principal person if they are the ones achieving the best results. We did deal with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You told all that to Mr. Hannis; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we talked about the problem, and it was quite clear from my statement that I named Ratko Markovic as the chief negotiator in a formal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, sir,. Please listen to my question. You say that on the 4th and 5th of November when you met with Mr. Hannis, you told him this was an incorrect phraseology and use of the word "principal negotiator." Is that what you're saying? That's what I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis himself initiated the issue, and I was quite willing to have it clarified. And Mr. Hannis had this information that I felt that there was a difference in the genius of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mr. Tanic, we received a document. The document I'm holding in my hand right here, please look at it. I'm holding it in my hand up here, to your left. Sir, I'm standing to your left. Look at me, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to sit like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm just saying -- I'm asking you to look at me. I'm holding a document in my hand, and it's a supplemental information sheet that the Prosecutor gave us, after his meeting with you on the 4th and 5th of November this year. And nowhere in this statement is there any reference to a correction or addition in relation to the words we're talking about. Now, you didn't -- either Mr. Hannis has misled us or you're not telling the truth right now. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll stipulate that that's not in the supplemental information, but it doesn't necessarily follow that I misled him or the witness is lying. There's another possibility. Mr. Hannis was neglectful.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's go one step further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, it will also give you one opportunity or avenue, at least, of clarifying some part of this before you proceed further on it. Mr. Tanic, that completes our session for today. Regrettably, we have not time to continue. Another case will be in this courtroom in the afternoon, so you will have to return to continue your evidence tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Please remember what I said to you on Friday. It's vital not to have any discussion about the evidence with anyone at all. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the -- oh, sorry, we'll go into closed session before we invite you to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request that we retrieve the bundle of documents from the witness and statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you leave the courtroom, Mr. Tanic, just leave everything that was provided in the court on the table, and it will be dealt with once you've left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
